---
engine: markdown
title: "Show a trend inside a cell"
subtitle: "Sparklines and bars sharing one scale down the column."
description: "format-nanoplot draws a series inside a table cell, with the domain taken from the whole column so the rows can be compared."
---

A column of series is a column of shapes, and a reader compares them by eye.
`format-nanoplot` draws each cell through whichever renderer is passed, and the domain is shared down the column so the comparison means something.

```{typst}
//| file: ../../tests/visual/nanoplots.typ
//| echo: true
//| alt: "A portfolio table with a sparkline and a bar plot per row, the asset name and the weight centred against the plots beside them: equities rising, bonds falling, and cash nearly flat."
```

Cash reads as flat because all three rows share one scale, taken from the column itself rather than passed in.
Scaled per cell, its small wobble would draw exactly like the others' real movement, which is how a nanoplot lies.

A plot is taller than the figures beside it, so `cell-vertical-align` decides where the short cells sit.
Typst puts a table cell at the top of its row, and `horizon` centres each one against the tallest cell beside it.

The two renderers differ on where they measure from.
`nanoplot-bar()` measures from zero, since a bar drawn from 5 to 10 makes a small difference look like the whole quantity.
`nanoplot-line()` scales to the domain, since a trend is about shape rather than magnitude.

`format-nanoplot` takes any `(numbers, domain: none, width: .., height: ..) => content`, so a renderer written in the document works exactly as well as the three that ship.
A nanoplot column holds readings rather than quantities, so it cannot be summarised, and `columns: auto` leaves it out.
